Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, hypervigilance can be coherent, but specifically scanning for weapons or dangerous objects points to an interpersonal/assaultive threat context rather than chemical contamination. This threat item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type and with the memory items, which are sensory and exposure-based rather than assault-related.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: Sexual coping is not impossible, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile. The active formulation is dominated by Memory–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies links around re-experiencing and danger, while the other strategy items are broad avoidance/denial. This item addresses tension reduction in a way not otherwise represented by the triggers, threat, or memory content, making the profile less clinically coherent.

vignette:
Priya Mehta is a 50-year-old South Asian woman who has worked as a diplomat for over two decades, spending much of her career navigating high-stakes negotiations and international postings with a composure her colleagues had always found remarkable. She is single, having long ago made a kind of peace with the fact that her career left little room for the domestic rhythms that sustained other people. She presented for treatment approximately eight months after a toxic chemical exposure at a diplomatic reception in a foreign capital - an incident that, she told the intake clinician with careful precision, she was still not entirely sure had been as serious as others seemed to think.

The incident itself occurred during a formal evening event at an embassy residence. Priya had been standing near a ventilation corridor when an unidentified chemical agent - later determined to be an organophosphate compound released through the building's climate control system - began affecting guests in the immediate area. She recalled the onset as almost imperceptible: a faint, acrid sweetness at the back of her throat, like something between burnt almonds and industrial solvent, followed within minutes by a tightening in her chest, blurred vision, and a profound sense that her body was no longer obeying her. She remembered the taste most of all - sharp and chemical and wrong in a way that no food or drink had ever been - because it arrived before she understood what was happening, before fear had a name to attach itself to. Several guests required hospitalisation. Priya was treated and discharged within forty-eight hours and returned to her duties within the week, which she had taken as evidence that she was fine.

In the months that followed, however, she found that her body had not received the same memo. She described a persistent physical vigilance - a tightness across her shoulders and jaw that never fully released, a readiness in her muscles that she could not switch off even in moments of objective safety. At receptions, which her role required her to attend regularly, she found herself moving slowly through rooms, reading the air conditioning vents, watching other guests for signs of distress, cataloguing exits. She could not have articulated a specific threat she was looking for; she was simply looking. At a multilateral conference in Geneva six months after the incident, a colleague's perfume - something floral with a chemical topnote - brought the full memory back without transition or warning: the taste arrived first, exactly as it had that evening, and she was briefly, completely, back in the ventilation corridor with her vision narrowing. She excused herself and stood in a bathroom stall for eleven minutes before she felt able to re-enter the room.

Priya had begun, quietly and without naming it as such, to restructure her professional life around the avoidance of situations she categorised as potentially stressful. She declined two posting offers that would have required her to attend large formal events regularly. She stopped reading the incident reports that circulated within her department about chemical and biological threats, forwarding them unread to a junior colleague. When the memory pressed in during quiet moments - on the metro, in the early hours of the morning - she found herself insisting inwardly that it had not been a significant event, that she had been treated and cleared and that other people had been far more affected. She had come to rely on this reasoning as a kind of handrail. Yet when she tried to describe the incident in any formal context - a security debrief, a conversation with her physician - she found she could not hold the thread of it. The sequence dissolved. She would begin and then lose the architecture of what she was trying to say, arriving at silence with no clear sense of how she had gotten there.

What finally brought her to seek help was a performance review in which her supervisor, gently but explicitly, noted that she had become less available, less willing to engage with the operational demands of her role. Priya had sat with that observation for three weeks before making the appointment. What she feared most, she said at intake, was that something had changed in her permanently. What she hoped for, with a diplomat's careful understatement, was to get back to being useful.
